name: Delaware Bay and Bombay Hook
blurb: Horseshoe crab eggs fuel red knots on a tidal marsh shore.

tip.title: Take away the crabs
tip.text: Horseshoe crabs lay their eggs on the beaches in spring. Set Horseshoe crab to -100% and watch the red knots and gulls lose their food.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Bombay Hook National Wildlife Refuge

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.desc: Dominant grass of the seaward salt marsh. It traps sediment and builds the marsh edge, and snow geese dig up its rhizomes.
Tall reed that forms dense stands in brackish and freshwater marsh. Muskrats and ducks use it for food and cover.

nodes.name: Diatoms and dinoflagellates
nodes.desc: Microscopic algae drifting in the bay and tidal creeks. They feed filter-feeders such as mussels.
Common hardwood of the refuge uplands and wooded swamp. Its seeds are eaten by squirrels and goldfinches.
Filter-feeding marsh bivalve that eats phytoplankton and bacteria. Birds, raccoons and blue crabs eat it.
Winter visitor that gathers in huge flocks at the refuge. It pulls up cordgrass rhizomes in the marsh.
Marsh rodent that eats reeds and other aquatic plants and builds lodges. Prey for foxes, raccoons and eagles.
Abundant dabbling duck on the managed pools and tidal creeks. It eats seeds and marsh plants.
Common in the refuge woods, where it eats seeds and nuts such as sweetgum fruit.
Long-distance shorebird that stops on the bay to feast on horseshoe crab eggs and nearly doubles its weight.
Omnivore of marsh and woods. It eats muskrats, ducks, squirrels and ribbed mussels.
Soaring scavenger that cleans up carcasses of mammals and birds across the refuge.
Threatened species at the refuge that takes ducks, geese, gulls and muskrats.
Common refuge predator that eats muskrats, ducks, squirrels and raccoons.
Drives growth of marsh grasses and plankton in the shallow bay.
Spring tides flood the marsh and let female horseshoe crabs spawn at the high-water line.

nodes.name: Decomposers
nodes.desc: Bacteria and fungi break down dead marsh grass and carcasses, returning nutrients to the mud.

link_ideas.with: Red knot (South America and the Arctic)
link_ideas.what: Rufa red knots stop in Delaware Bay on migration between wintering grounds in South America and Arctic breeding grounds.
